Breeze of Breslov

Parashas Vayigash | Dec10th-11th 2021

The Greatest Comfort 

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus

In Parashat Vayigash, an epic confrontation takes place between two of the most compelling figures in the Torah. Yehuda, the courageous and unquestioned leader of the Children of Yaakov, aggressively approaches Yosef, the charismatic and dynamic younger brother who’s life had inexplicably transformed from that of intense personal suffering and servitude to that of unparalleled spiritual mastery and universal influence. 

The most gripping part of this showdown is that Yehuda does not actually know he is speaking to Yosef, for he had not seen his younger brother in 17 years. Instead, Yehuda thought he was speaking to the harsh and unsympathetic viceroy of a foreign kingdom. At the apex of Yehuda’s frustration, he even told Yosef he was like “Pharaoh,” the ruthless militant leader of an unjust society. 

At the very same time, Yosef knew exactly who he was speaking to. As the Torah states regarding this unusual dynamic, “Yosef recognized his brothers, but his brothers did not recognize him.” 

Following the impassioned pleading of Yehuda, Yosef had to forcibly remove himself from the conversation. Due to the aching pain welling up in Yosef’s heart at the sight of his brother’s distress, Yosef excused himself to a private room where he proceeded to weep with great intensity. Afterwards, Yosef washed his face and came back out to continue his charade of indifference. 

This mysterious back and forth is something our Sages go to great lengths to explain. However, it was not until my late Rabbi Aharon Walkin Ztl revealed something to me that made me realize the life changing depth of this entire interaction. 

Based on a powerful Midrash, Rav Walkin explained that Yosef composed himself as a harsh and distant authority figure only to afford his brothers the opportunity to achieve genuine teshuva. Iwas an act rooted in the ultimate level of empathy. One in whichno one else would be capable of carrying out, as it required the 

deepest level of maturity, emotional awareness, and genuine selflessness to perform. For without this external facade on the part of Yosef, his brothers would not have been able to rectify the egregious error they made two decades earlier in exiling Yosef from his own home and estranging him from the only family he ever knew. 

The fundamental point Rav Walkin added to this Midrash, and one in which Rebbe Nachman similarly expounds on as well, is that just as Yosef is the archetypal “Tzaddik Yesod Olam,” the 

central figure on whom the entire world stands, he is only a mere reflection and window into the ultimate “Tzaddik Yesod Olam,” HaShem himself. That is to say, that the entire drama between Yosef and his brothers is really an exact parallel to the drama currently unfolding between HaShem and us. 

Therefore, the painful experiences we have all endured in our lives, the private grudges we have developed and continue to harbor, and the heartfelt pleading we have since engaged in withHaShem, are all reflected by Yehuda approaching Yosef. 

HaShem’s seeming “indifference” to our plight is really nothing other than the rich soil from which our individual heroism will ultimately blossom. HaShem’s ability to withhold his true intentions and feelings, are paradoxically His greatest compassion.

But be sure of this. Just as Yehuda before us, if we refuse to give up and continuously approach Him, one day soon we will also get to hear the truth. 

“I’m Yosef.” 

And in the meantime, while we are trying to muster up the courage to continue fighting, remember and meditate deeply on this point. 

While you are in distress, HaShem is not just listening. He is also crying with you. 

This is actually the greatest comfort of all. 

Shabbat Shalom.

Ga’ula at the Heart of Galus

Aaron London, RN, BSN

Reb Yossi Katz, in his sefer The Rebbe’s Shabbos Table, shares with us the following teaching based on the writings of Reb Nosson of Breslov in Likutey Halachos, Yoreh Deah, Hilchos Shluach HaKen, Halachah Heh, Sections 23-24: Yaakov decides to sojourn to Mitzrayim (Egypt) after learning that Yosef is still alive. Prior to his departure, Hashem says to him, “I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up…” (46:4). The concept of “going down to Mitzrayim” does not just mean in a physical sense. Rather, as Reb Yossi explains, “going down to Mitzrayim” conveys the notion of Yaakov’s descent into exile and the resulting trepidation he felt (p. 69). Mitzrayim comes from the language of constriction and, therefore, on the level of penimiyus, the Torah is teaching us that Yaakov was moving from the expanded experience of self represented by Eretz Yisroel to the exiled experience of self represented by Mitzrayim. Reb Nosson writes towards the beginning of section 23 that the essential expression of galus Yisroel is the galus hanefesh. He explains, “All ascensions and descentions that occur to a Jewish man is the essential secret of galus (exile) and ga’ula (redemption)… which is the concept of a descent for the sake of an ascent” (p. 286). Therefore, R’ Nosson’s reading of the aforementioned pasuk teaches us that galus / descension is the necessary groundwork for ga’ula / ascension. 

At the heart of the above teaching is a paradigm that I often share with the people I work with in substance abuse. It is a paradigm that I myself have been working for many years to 

inculcate into my being and this paradigm emerges out of the following question: when it comes to emotional and psychological well-being, how do we relate to our inner worlds? How do we relate to ourselves when we experience the inevitable “lows” of daily living? Do we fester negative feelings towards ourselves? Is there guilt? Do we harbor residual feelings that blunt our ability to move forward? Or, alternatively, do we recognize that ebbs and flows are intrinsic to the human experience? If we understand that ebbs and flows are part and parcel to what it means to be human, then the gift that we offer ourselves is the gift of buoyancy and fluidity anchored in our acknowledgment that true growth involves ups and downs. 

One of my teachers shared with me the following metaphor which I believe captures the essence of the idea. Imagine that there are two people standing on a beach. The waves pull one person into the ocean, while the other person is able to stay grounded in the sand. What is the difference between these two people? Not that one person is experiencing the waves and the other is not. They both are experiencing the waves. Rather, the key difference is that one is able to stabilize himself in the presence of the water, while the other is not. 

The reason this metaphor is profound is because it conveys that mental heath does not mean someone is perfect without issues. Rather, the true barometer of mental health is a person’s ability to make a space for the waves of his inner world. Do these waves overwhelm me or is my sense of self bigger than the waves themselves? Herein lies the depth of R’ Nosson’s teaching. When I understand that my experience of galus, in whatever expression that takes, is not reflective of something wrong with me, but rather the fertile soil for my ultimately ga’ula, then I have learned the secret of how to stay standing on the beach. 

At that point, a person no longer has to be afraid because he has transformed his relationship to the experience of galus itself. 

Galus, therefore, is not something to run away from. Rather, together with Hashem, we walk into galus only to discover that the derech to ga’ula is traversed specifically through the vulnerability and courage that galus engenders. 

Gut Shabbos, 

ALY
